fixes.explanation: No servant shows up anywhere in this scene. The man says, “Lord, have mercy on my son…” and then describes what the boy is suffering. I think his whole heart is with his child.

The man says the opposite. He tells Jesus, “I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.” So the man says the disciples could not heal his son. He is kneeling in front of Jesus when he says it.

That's right. The man tells Jesus, “I brought him to Your disciples, but they could not heal him.” So he brought his son to the disciples first, and they could not heal him. Now he is the one kneeling in front of Jesus.

Jesus doesn't point the dad toward a priest or anyone else. He says, “Bring the boy here to Me.” Right after His strong words, the boy is what He turns to. I think that tells us those words weren't the end of the story for that boy.

No waiting is mentioned in this passage. Jesus says, “Bring the boy here to Me.” Then Jesus rebuked the demon, and the boy was healed from that moment (Matthew 17:18). Nothing gets put off until tomorrow.

Nobody asks that here, friend. The disciples come to Jesus privately and ask, “Why couldn’t we drive it out?” I think that sounds like people looking at themselves, not questioning Jesus. Jesus answers them with, “Because you have so little faith…”

Sand sounds like a good guess, but Jesus doesn't use it. He says, “…if you have faith the size of a mustard seed…” That seed-sized faith is the kind He says can speak to a mountain: “…you can say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move.” Sand never comes up.

Jesus says, “They will kill Him…” This is a heavy one, and I think it was hard for the disciples to hear. He is saying it about Himself, since the Son of Man is the name He uses for Himself (Mark 2:10).

The collectors ask Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” They bring the question to Peter, but it's about his Teacher. Peter is the one who gets asked. Jesus is the one the question is about.
The collectors don't ask about the whole group. They ask Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, “Does your Teacher pay the two drachmas?” The collectors name one person, and it's Jesus.
Peter answers, “Yes.” That's his response when the collectors ask if his Teacher pays the two drachmas. After that, Peter enters the house, and Jesus speaks to him first.
The text says the opposite. When the collectors ask whether his Teacher pays, Peter answers, “Yes.” Then Peter enters the house, where Jesus speaks to him first.

Jesus tells Peter that when he opens the mouth of the first fish he catches, he will find “…a four-drachma coin.” Then Jesus says, “Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.” A coin is exactly what Jesus names.

Jesus covers more than just His own. He tells Peter, “Take it and give it to them for My tax and yours.” So the coin is meant for both of them. Peter's tax is included too, and Jesus says he'll find the coin in a fish's mouth.
